notes:
I've written notes for every verse, but the sources are thinner than I'd like. I ran out of searches before reaching the Pulpit Commentary, preceptaustin's pages for most verses, netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org or oca.org. So there is no modern-scholarship or Orthodox material here, and the only Catholic source is catholic.com on v. 9. For verses 13–23, the traditional reading comes mostly from David Guzik (Enduring Word) and John Wesley's Notes. The two places where traditions clearly differ are v. 8 and v. 24.

**v. 1**
- "Therefore" follows on from 1 Peter 1's teaching on God's eternal word. The vices listed describe the kind of heart that can receive the word: humble, honest and willing to obey. The word "slander" ("evil speaking") means hurtful gossip more than swearing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-2/
- Wesley: these sins must be put off because they don't fit with the pure love of 1:22. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/2.htm
- Bob Deffinbaugh (bible.org): "putting aside" is a supporting step that prepares for the one real command, "long for the milk." You cannot keep malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy and slander and still desire the Word. https://bible.org/seriespage/8-enduring-word-1-peter-122-23

**v. 2**
- The Greek word for "crave" is strong. The Greek Old Testament uses it for the soul panting after God (Psalm 42:1). Healthy babies want milk without being told. Guzik adds that in a sense even the most mature believers are still "babes." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-2/
- The Word is both the "seed" by which we were born again (1:23) and the "milk" by which we grow. In 2:2 salvation is not the starting point but the goal that obeying the Word moves us toward. https://bible.org/seriespage/8-enduring-word-1-peter-122-23
- Wesley: the milk is God's word, which feeds the soul and deceives no one. The aim is growth in faith, love and holiness toward full maturity in Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/2.htm

**v. 3**
- "Tasted" means personally experienced. Having tasted God's kindness gives believers both reason and duty to take in the word eagerly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-2/
- Wesley: known sweetly and by experience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/2.htm
- bible.org notes Peter's thinking here draws heavily on Psalm 34. https://bible.org/seriespage/8-enduring-word-1-peter-122-23

**v. 4**
- Jesus is the first "living stone." Believers are living stones because they are joined to Him, the source of life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-2/
- Wesley: we come to Him by faith. Christ is "living" from eternity and risen from the dead. Wesley says Peter's words show he saw Christ, not himself, as the rock the church is built on. He adds that Christ is still rejected today, including by nominal Christians who trust in their own works. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/2.htm

**v. 5**
- As Israel had a temple, priests and sacrifices, the church has a spiritual temple (believers themselves), a holy priesthood and spiritual sacrifices. Each believer can come to God directly, with no mediator but Jesus, and serves as a priest only through Him. God is building believers *together*. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-2/
- Wesley: the spiritual sacrifices are our souls and bodies, with all our thoughts, words and actions. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/2.htm

**v. 6**
- Guzik lists the Old Testament "stone" texts that point to Christ: Psalm 118:22, Isaiah 8:14, Isaiah 28:16, Daniel 2 and the rock in the wilderness (1 Corinthians 10:4). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-2/
- Wesley: believers will not be put to shame, either in this life or in eternity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/2.htm

**v. 7**
- If Christ is precious to someone, that is a sign of true faith. Spurgeon preached his first sermon on this verse at 16. Guzik notes G. Campbell Morgan preferred the Revised Version, "for you … is the preciousness": believers share in Christ's honour. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-2/
- In Guzik's reading, Christ as cornerstone, joining two walls, sets the course for Jew and Gentile to become one house. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-2/

**v. 8 — where traditions differ ("to this they were appointed")**
- **John Gill (Calvinist Baptist):** God appointed some both to stumble and to the unbelief that causes it. He chose to leave them in the disobedience they fell into, and they justly perish. Others are objects of "distinguishing grace." (Gill) https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/glt/1-peter/2-8.html
- **Adam Clarke (Methodist):** those who do not believe were appointed to stumble and fall by the word, not appointed to disbelieve it. Nothing suggests they were decreed to disobey. (Clarke) https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/glt/1-peter/2-8.html
- **John Wesley (Methodist):** the appointment is God's eternal decree that "he that believeth not shall be damned." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/2.htm
- **Albert Barnes (Presbyterian):** nobody can use this verse as an excuse. People know they reject Christ willingly. They are not forced; God saw what would happen and sent the Saviour anyway. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/glt/1-peter/2-8.html
- **Preceptaustin / Thomas Constable (evangelical):** the verse teaches that all who willfully disobey the word are destined to stumble; "appointed" refers back to the whole clause. Their disobedience is not what God ordained, but the penalty for it is. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_peter_27-8
- **Guzik:** it is appointed that those who disobey the word should stumble over Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-2/

**v. 9 — where traditions differ (priesthood)**
- Titles that once belonged to Israel alone now belong to every Christian. In Christ, kingship and priesthood, kept separate in Israel, come together. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-2/
- **Reformed:** The Gospel Coalition says Christians don't depend on church priests to interpret Scripture or secure forgiveness for them; all are equally priests through Christ. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/the-priesthood-of-all-believers/ Ligonier says God is no more accessible to clergy than to laypeople, and that whole lives, including jobs, are offered to God. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/gods-royal-priesthood
- **Catholic:** Christians are priests, but Scripture also shows a special, ministerial priesthood. 1 Peter 2:9 refers to the common priesthood. https://www.catholic.com/audio/ddp/the-priesthood-of-all-believers A second catholic.com episode argues that Peter is applying to the Church what was earlier said of Israel, which also had a separate priesthood. https://www.catholic.com/audio/tjap/n-t-wright-the-priesthood-of-all-believers
- **Ellicott (older Anglican commentary):** the verse quotes Exodus 19:6. Priestly status belonged to all Israel under the Law, as it does to the whole new Israel, and he says this bears on how we think about church ministry. "Proclaim" means telling outsiders what has happened inside. God chose His people not for their own sake but to make Him known. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/2-9.htm
- **Wesley:** "royal" means power with God and victory over sin, the world and the devil. "Priests" means consecrated to offer spiritual sacrifices. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/2.htm

**v. 10**
- In Guzik's reading, this was a great relief for Gentiles: "you used to not belong, but now you belong to God." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-2/
- Wesley: the first half of the verse is mainly about Gentiles, the second about Jews. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/2.htm

**v. 11**
- We can only resist the desires of the flesh if we live as people whose home is heaven. The battle lasts as long as we live. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-2/
- Wesley: "sojourners" are people living in someone else's house, "pilgrims" people in a foreign country. You sojourn in the body and are a pilgrim in this world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/2.htm

**v. 12**
- Early Christians were falsely accused of cannibalism, orgies and atheism. They answered the slander mainly by living visibly righteous lives, not by argument. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-2/
- Wesley: the "day of visitation" is when God offers them His mercy again. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/2.htm

**vv. 13–14**
- Governments have rightful authority from God, so we must obey them unless they command something against God's law. God sends rulers to punish wrongdoers and recognise those who do good. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-2/
- Wesley: rulers are set up by people as the means, but all their power comes originally from God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/2.htm

**v. 15**
- People who never read the Bible will read our lives. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-2/
- Wesley: the critics' "ignorance" means they don't really know Christians, which is a strong reason to pity them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/2.htm

**v. 16**
- Our liberty in Jesus is no excuse for sin; we use it to show love and respect. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-2/

**v. 17**
- Wesley: honour everyone because they are made in God's image, bought by His Son and meant for His kingdom. Honour the king as far as God's law and man's law require. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/2.htm

**vv. 18–20**
- Guzik applies the passage to employers. Submission applies even to harsh masters, and enduring unjust treatment patiently is commendable before God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-2/
- Wesley: the word means household servants. "Fear" means fear of offending them or God. "Conscious of God" means a pure desire to please Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/2.htm

**vv. 21–23**
- Jesus is the example of someone punished unjustly who did not hit back but entrusted Himself to the Father. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-2/
- Wesley: Christ's example especially suits servants, who are tempted to deceit, insults and threats. Trusting the righteous Judge is "the only solid ground of patience in affliction." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/2.htm

**v. 24 — where traditions differ ("by His stripes you are healed")**
- **Traditional reading:** Christ is far more than an example. He bore our sins as a substitute, and "tree" means the cross. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-2/ Calvin calls Christ's death a sacrifice to pay for our sins: He took our sin and our punishment on Himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-peter/2-24.html Wesley says Christ bore the punishment our sins deserved, on the cross where mainly slaves were executed. Without atonement for guilt we could never be freed from sin's power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/2.htm
- **What "healed" means, in older commentators:** several connect it to beaten slaves. Christ, by bearing stripes (a punishment for slaves), healed them of much worse wounds: guilt of conscience and defilement of soul. Barnes says sin is often pictured as a disease, and redemption as recovery from a deadly illness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/2-24.htm
- **Pentecostal (Assemblies of God):** deliverance from sickness is provided in the atonement and is the privilege of all believers. Their position paper agrees that Isaiah and 1 Peter 2:24–25 emphasize especially healing from sin. But because Isaiah 53:4 stresses physical sickness, they hold the gospel heals both spiritual and physical effects of the fall. Healing now is a foretaste of the coming redemption of the body. https://ag.org/Beliefs/Position-Papers/Divine-Healing
- **Critics of the popular "claim your healing" teaching:** Constable calls it non-biblical to say Jesus' death made healing from any physical ailment something every Christian can claim in this life. The context of Isaiah 53 and the past tense "were healed" point to spiritual healing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-peter/2-24.html Got Questions says the verse is about sin and righteousness, not sickness and disease. https://www.gotquestions.org/by-His-stripes-healed.html Ligonier (Reformed) tells of a man who took the verse from things he read online as a promise his wife would be healed, and she died. It teaches spiritual healing now, with bodily healing guaranteed on the last day. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/his-stripes-we-are-healed

**v. 25**
- Wesley: "Bishop" (BSB "Overseer") means the kind observer, inspector or overseer of souls. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/2.htm
- Barclay translates it as the "Shepherd and Watchman" of your souls.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-peter/2-24.html
